# TEB-Veg and TEB-Hydro: representing water processes in the urban fabric

![](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/4175/2018/gmd-11-4175-2018-f01.png){.project-hero fig-alt="Conceptual schematic of hydrological processes represented by the TEB-Hydro model, from Stavropulos-Laffaille et al. (2018)"}

<small>Figure from Stavropulos-Laffaille et al. (2018), distributed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).</small>

::: {.project-meta}
**Research area:** applied mathematics · urban hydrology · environmental modelling  
**Scientific output:** peer-reviewed article, *Geoscientific Model Development* (2018)  
**Model framework:** Town Energy Balance (TEB) · SURFEX v7.3  
**Evaluation context:** two small residential catchments in Nantes, France
:::

## Research question

Cities change how rainfall is intercepted, stored, infiltrated, evaporated, and routed to drainage networks. These water transfers interact with urban energy exchanges and microclimate. To assess adaptation strategies such as green infrastructure, urban models need to represent water processes across both vegetated and built surfaces.

The Town Energy Balance (TEB) model is an urban-canopy model within the [SURFEX surface modelling platform](https://cnrm.sedoo.fr/surfex-2/). TEB-Veg extended the urban representation to include vegetation within street canyons. However, the hydrological representation of soil beneath built surfaces and its interaction with surface water remained incomplete. The TEB-Hydro development addressed this gap by extending the urban water budget to the subsoil under built surfaces and connecting soil-water processes to drainage.

For the model background, see the [CNRM overview of TEB](https://cnrm.sedoo.fr/teb-town-energy-balance/) and the foundational paper on [including vegetation in TEB](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-5-1377-2012).

## What changed in the model?

The paper introduces **TEB-Hydro**, a more complete hydrological representation built on TEB-Veg. Its principal developments include:

- **Subsoil beneath built surfaces:** represent soil-water processes below impervious urban surfaces rather than treating the built surface as hydrologically disconnected from the underlying soil.
- **Within-grid soil-moisture redistribution:** rebalance soil moisture horizontally within a model grid cell.
- **Drainage to the sewer network:** represent the routing of soil water into urban drainage.
- **Limited deep drainage:** constrain deep drainage to improve the water-budget representation.
- **Parameter sensitivity and calibration:** analyse which hydrological parameters most affect simulated discharge and need calibration.

These changes connect urban surface representation to a more explicit water budget. They are particularly relevant when assessing nature-based solutions, where changes to vegetation and soil can affect both water transfers and energy exchanges.

## Evaluation and results

The study evaluates the model on **two small residential catchments in Nantes**, over two distinct periods, by comparing simulated sewer discharge with observations. It includes a sensitivity analysis to identify hydrological parameters relevant to calibration.

The published results report several important qualifications:

- The model tends to **overestimate total sewer discharge** in both catchments.
- Performance is better in wet-weather conditions, with a **Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) above 0.80**, compared with approximately **0.60 in drier conditions**.
- The authors identify the same parameter set for both catchments despite differences in meteorological and local physical conditions.

The results are promising, but not uniformly strong across weather regimes. In particular, the dry-weather performance and discharge overestimation matter when interpreting the model's use for impact assessment. The paper presents the work as a step towards city-scale studies alongside climate and demographic projections, not as proof that every urban hydrological condition is already represented without bias.

## Related research and resources

The work is part of a broader development of urban surface models. The following resources help place it in context.

### Directly related TEB-Hydro work

- **Stavropulos-Laffaille et al. (2017), “Hydrological validation of an urban hydro-microclimate model (TEB-Hydro): Sensitivity analysis on the catchment of Rezé (Nantes, France).”** *La Houille Blanche*, 103(3), 14–21. This earlier validation paper focuses on sensitivity analysis for the Rezé catchment and is directly relevant to the 2018 model evaluation. [Publication DOI](https://doi.org/10.1051/lhb/2017017) · [HAL record](https://hal.science/hal-05325715)
- **Source code and run directories for the 2018 paper.** The research artefact is archived on Zenodo, providing a reproducibility trail beyond the article itself. [Zenodo record, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1218016](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1218016)

### Foundational and adjacent TEB research

- **Lemonsu et al. (2012), “Inclusion of vegetation in the Town Energy Balance model for modelling urban green areas.”** Describes the integration of vegetation into the urban canyon and evaluation against field observations. [*Geoscientific Model Development*](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-5-1377-2012)
- **de Munck et al. (2013), “The GREENROOF module (v7.3) for modelling green roof hydrological and energetic performances within TEB.”** Extends TEB to represent the water and energy exchanges of extensive green roofs, an adjacent but distinct application from the TEB-Hydro catchment work. [*Geoscientific Model Development*](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-6-1941-2013)
- **TEB model overview and bibliography.** The CNRM page provides model context and references to other TEB developments. [CNRM TEB overview](https://cnrm.sedoo.fr/teb-town-energy-balance/)
- **SURFEX platform overview.** Describes the wider surface-modelling system in which TEB is integrated. [CNRM SURFEX overview](https://cnrm.sedoo.fr/surfex-2/)
- **TEB model code and documentation.** [Source repository](https://github.com/teb-model/teb) · [Documentation](https://teb-model.github.io/teb/)

## Methods and transferable lessons

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.method-card}
### Process-based modelling
Make assumptions about physical processes explicit and encode them as model components.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Sensitivity analysis
Identify parameters that materially affect model outputs before interpreting calibration results.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Evaluation against observations
Compare simulated sewer discharge with measured data across catchments and weather regimes.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Error-aware interpretation
Report systematic overestimation and performance differences rather than relying on a single aggregate metric.
:::
:::

For me, this research sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, environmental processes, numerical modelling, and scientific software. It also illustrates a general principle that carries over to Data Science and AI evaluation: a model should be assessed against observations, under relevant operating conditions, with limitations and failure modes made visible.

## Evidence and attribution

The primary evidence is the [2018 peer-reviewed article](https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-11-4175-2018), its [review record](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/4175/2018/gmd-11-4175-2018-discussion.html), and its [archived code and run directories](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1218016). Related publications provide historical and technical context; they are not presented as work authored by me unless I am listed among their authors.
